People come to the Yijing expecting a verdict. Will the deal close, will the move go well, should I wait. The text looks like it will answer: 元亨，利貞; 不利東北; 有攸往. It reads like a fortune slip.

It isn't one. The Yizhuan — the ten commentaries that turn a divination manual into a book of philosophy — does something more specific: it marks position and boundary, and it declines to convert them into luck.

## What a line actually says

Take the top line of Qian: 亢龍有悔.

Standard translations give "the arrogant dragon will have cause for regret" — a warning, a prediction of bad outcome. But 亢 is not "arrogant" in the moral sense. It means raised to the extreme, high and exposed, at the limit of ascent. 悔 is not punishment; it is the friction that follows when a position has passed its own measure.

The line is not saying "you will be unlucky." It is saying: at this position, the thing has nowhere left to rise, and the structure will begin to press back. Whether that is bad depends on what you do next. The text marks the boundary; it does not grade it.

Once you read lines this way, the whole book changes register. 吉 and 凶 stop being rewards and punishments handed down by fortune and become readings of fit: does this action match this position, at this time, with these others. 无咎 — "no blame" — is not "safe." It is "the action leaves nothing to answer for," which is a different and much stricter standard.

## 合 and 和 are not the same thing

The distinction the Yizhuan keeps making is between 合 and 和.

合 is人为之合: unification by force of will. It works on sameness — press differences into one shape, bring disagreement under one heading, and the result looks orderly. The cost is that the differences are gone, and with them the information they carried.

和 is 天道之和: harmony by position. It works on placement — different things each hold their own place, and none needs to become the other. Five flavors make a meal; five tones make music. Nobody blends them into one flavor or one pitch.

The six lines of a hexagram are a 和 structure, not a 合 structure. They are not equal, not interchangeable, and not reducible to each other. Line 2 is the minister's place, line 5 the ruler's; the same action that fits one is wrong at the other. What makes the hexagram coherent is that each line stays in its position and responds to its neighbors, not that all six agree.

This is why the Yizhuan refuses the verdict form. A verdict is a 合 move: it collapses a situation into one word, and the word then replaces the situation. 吉 or 凶 is exactly that collapse. The commentary would rather leave you with the position and let you carry the judgment.

## A hexagram is never alone

The text also builds relation into the reading. Each hexagram is read through three neighbors:

- 综卦 (inverted): the same six lines read upside down. What looks like advance from one end looks like retreat from the other.
- 错卦 (opposite): every line flipped. The situation's exact negation, which is often its hidden condition.
- 互卦 (interlaced): lines 2–4 and 3–5 form two inner hexagrams. The situation contains another situation inside it.

None of these are decoration. They are the mechanism by which a single hexagram stops being a snapshot and becomes a position in a field. You cannot read 乾 without seeing 坤; you cannot read a line without seeing what surrounds it.

## What this costs the reader

The Yizhuan asks more of you than a fortune slip does. It gives you 64 positions, 384 lines, and a set of relations, and then it asks you to locate yourself. That is slower, and it can be wrong. But it is checkable: you can be shown why a line fits or doesn't, and you can argue with it.

A verdict cannot be argued with. That is its appeal, and that is exactly what the commentary gives up.

## The book

72 卷, 50.5 万 characters, v1.50.0. Base text follows Wang Bi, checked against the Zhouyi Zhengyi, the Zhouyi Benyi and the Zhouyi Jijie, with the Mawangdui silk manuscripts kept as variant readings. Every hexagram runs seven sections: base text, social background, character exegesis, line-by-line reading with Laozi and Zhuangzi cross-references, structural relations (inverted, opposite, interlaced), 合与和, and common misreadings. Print PDF: 704 pages.
